### Problem: Petr and a Combination Lock {#sec-cx-p1-lock}

::: {.p-statement}
A lock dial starts at 0 on a 360-degree scale. Petr must make $n$ rotations ($1 \le n \le 15$) of $a_i$ degrees ($1 \le a_i \le 180$), each either clockwise or counterclockwise. Print `YES` if some choice of directions brings the pointer back to 0, otherwise `NO`.

Source: [CF 1097B · Petr and a Combination Lock](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1097/B){.solved rating="1200"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
$n \le 15$ is the hint: $2^{15} = 32768$ direction choices, each checked in $O(n)$, is about $5\cdot10^5$ steps. No cleverness is needed; the small bound **is** the solution.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. Enumerate every mask $s \in [0, 2^n)$; bit $i$ set means rotation $i$ is clockwise.
2. Compute $\sum \pm a_i \bmod 360$; if it is 0 for any mask, answer `YES`.

**Alternative.** Track the set of reachable angles after each rotation (at most 360 of them): $O(360\,n)$. This scales to $n = 10^5$, and it is *pseudo-polynomial* (@sec-cx-budget): it depends on the value 360, not just on $n$.
:::

::: {#fig-cx-lock}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def lock_tree(a, i=0, s=0):
    if i == len(a):
        return V.Node(str(s), color="green" if s % 360 == 0 else "muted")
    kids = [lock_tree(a, i + 1, s + a[i]), lock_tree(a, i + 1, s - a[i])]
    kids[0].edge, kids[1].edge = f"+{a[i]}", f"−{a[i]}"
    return V.Node(str(s), kids, color="indigo")
def leaves(v):
    return [v] if not v.children else [x for c in v.children for x in leaves(c)]
t = lock_tree([10, 20, 30])
assert sum(int(v.label) % 360 == 0 for v in leaves(t)) == 2
def draw(ax, p):
    V.tree(ax, p, lock_tree([10, 20, 30]), dx=1.25, dy=1.6, size=10)
V.show(draw)
```

All 2^3 direction choices for rotations 10, 20, 30, as a tree of running totals. Two leaves are multiples of 360 (green), so the answer is YES. With n ≤ 15 the tree has at most 32768 leaves.

:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
#### Python

```{python}
#| label: cx-lock
def lock_bruteforce(a):
    n = len(a)
    for s in range(1 << n):
        total = sum(a[i] if s >> i & 1 else -a[i] for i in range(n))
        if total % 360 == 0:
            return "YES"
    return "NO"

def lock_reachable(a):
    reach = {0}
    for x in a:
        reach = {(r + x) % 360 for r in reach} | {(r - x) % 360 for r in reach}
    return "YES" if 0 in reach else "NO"

for _ in range(300):
    a = [random.randint(1, 180) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 10))]
    assert lock_bruteforce(a) == lock_reachable(a)

assert lock_bruteforce([10, 20, 30]) == "YES"
assert lock_bruteforce([10, 10, 10]) == "NO"
assert lock_bruteforce([120, 120, 120]) == "YES"
```

#### C++

```cpp
int main() {
    int n; cin >> n;
    vector<int> a(n);
    for (int& x : a) cin >> x;
    for (int s = 0; s < (1 << n); ++s) {
        int total = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) total += (s >> i & 1) ? a[i] : -a[i];
        if (((total % 360) + 360) % 360 == 0) { cout << "YES\n"; return 0; }
    }
    cout << "NO\n";
}
```
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Time** $O(2^n n)$, about $4.9\cdot10^5$ for $n = 15$. **Space** $O(1)$ for the enumeration, $O(360)$ for the reachable-set alternative.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- Negative remainders in C++: `-30 % 360 == -30`. Normalise with `((x % m) + m) % m`. Python's `%` is already non-negative.
- $n = 1$: one rotation of at most 180 degrees can never return to 0, so the answer is `NO`.
- $120 \times 3 = 360$: a full turn counts as 0.
:::
